extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, peer reviewers, research-integrity investigators, and publishers concerned with paper-mill fraud
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and investigative methods for identifying publications produced or brokered by paper mills, and editorial policies to detect/prevent fraudulent authorship and submissions. Covers both technical evidence-gathering and editorial safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal precedence
rubrics_metrics.description: To meet a high evidentiary standard of potential fraud, establish that the paper was made available for purchase before the article was published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Internet Archive (Wayback Machine) snapshots to show a paper title/ad listing predates the journal's publication (or submission) date. Treat temporal precedence as a strict criterion: without it, coincidental or copy listings are plausible. Note: scraped contracts may lack timestamps, so Wayback Machine snapshots are crucial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple indicators, not title matches alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Matching titles (exact or close) should be used only as one indicator among many when flagging potential paper-mill products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine title matches with other evidence (temporal precedence, author background, collaboration patterns, email domains, outlet characteristics) to reduce false positives due to coincidental similarity or title edits during review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author expertise and publication history
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether listed authors have a background in the paper’s topic area and a history of working together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of topical background or no prior collaboration between coauthors is suspicious and should increase scrutiny. Check authors' profiles, publication records, and institutional affiliations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspicious collaboration patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Unusual multi-institutional or multi-national author groupings can be an indicator of possible fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the collaboration is plausible given the research topic; odd geographic or institutional mixes with no prior shared work warrant further checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-institutional corresponding email addresses
rubrics_metrics.description: Corresponding authors using non-institutional emails (e.g., Gmail, Hotmail, Yahoo, QQ) are a red flag because paper mills can impersonate authors through such addresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify corresponding-author identity via institutional email when an institutional affiliation is claimed; treat non-institutional addresses with greater skepticism and seek additional verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outlet characteristics as risk factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers published in open-access journals, especially those with high volumes of output, are potential targets of paper mills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-volume OA journals and journals with lax editorial controls are higher risk. Use knowledge of journal practices and patterns (e.g., frequent special issues) to triage suspicious papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal/contract data from paper-mill listings
rubrics_metrics.description: Data contained in paper-mill contracts (titles, target indexing, cost, target publication date) provide structured evidence linking sold positions to published articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrape and parse HTML contracts where available; preserve copies for analysis. Even when contracts lack timestamps, other fields can help triangulate evidence when combined with Wayback snapshots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrape and archive paper-mill web content
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic scraping and archiving of paper-mill sites and Wayback snapshots enables reconstruction of deleted listings and supports temporal precedence claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scripted crawls and parsing (e.g., Python scripts) to collect contracts and archived snapshots; be aware Wayback snapshots are irregular, so some records may not be recoverable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for ghostwriting, brokering, and late-game authorships
rubrics_metrics.description: Services offered by mills—ghostwriting, selling authorship positions, and late changes to author lists—are core indicators of fraudulent publication practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate advertisements or evidence of those services; check for author additions late in the submission/publishing process and for editorial approvals of authorship changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special issues as a mechanism for fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements that tie papers to specific 'special issue' collections may indicate a coordinated mechanism for inserting mill-produced papers into journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a paper-mill listing references IDs or a batch of papers scheduled as a collection, check the corresponding journal issues for multiple near-identical or related papers and for suspicious groupings of authors/affiliations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-paper pattern analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Looking across multiple papers (rather than single-paper inspection) reveals patterns—textual templates, reuse of methods/figures, or recurring oddities—that make fraud more apparent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggregate and compare suspected papers for repeated phrases, figure reuse, similar methods, shared unusual errors, and consistent anomalous author patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documented editorial safeguards (recommended policy list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial policies that can mitigate paper-mill fraud include explicit rules on authorship changes, affiliation verification, reviewer selection, contribution statements, and ethical declarations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific recommended policies from the article: (1) Changes in authorship after submission must receive the editor’s approval and be made only under exceptional circumstances; (2) Corresponding authors who indicate an institutional affiliation must be verified by the author or supervisor using an email address from that institution; (3) All papers must be reviewed and approved by at least one reviewer that has a formal affiliation with the journal’s reviewer board or pool; (4) Authors must include a statement of their contributions, which is published with the final article; (5) Each author must sign a statement that their submission has met all ethical standards of the journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify corresponding-author institutional affiliation
rubrics_metrics.description: When a corresponding author claims an institutional affiliation, that affiliation should be verified via an institutional email or confirmation by the author/supervisor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require correspondence from an institutional address or documented verification; be aware this is not foolproof but raises the barrier to simple impersonation by mills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require reviewer with formal journal affiliation
rubrics_metrics.description: At least one reviewer approving a manuscript should have a formal affiliation with the journal’s reviewer board or pool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces the chance that journal-approved reviews are fabricated or conducted by complicit third parties; editors should maintain and check a vetted reviewer list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish author contribution statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must include a statement of their contributions that is published with the final article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making contribution statements public increases transparency and provides another data point for detecting inconsistencies with claimed work or with authors' expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require signed ethical compliance statements from each author
rubrics_metrics.description: Each author should sign a statement that their submission has met all ethical standards of the journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such statements should be required and retained; they are deterrents but are only meaningful if there are consequences for false attestations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial training and proactive detection
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should educate reviewers and editorial staff about paper mills and proactively adopt measures to detect fraudulent submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run internal workshops, rethink internal processes, develop blacklists of individuals/institutions connected to mills, and increase checks on author-group credentials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional judgment informed by field expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Use professional judgment and domain-specific knowledge about known paper-mill features when flagging suspicious papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigators and editors should rely on their knowledge of publication norms in the discipline to identify anomalies (e.g., implausible methods or authorship given topic). Combine this with documented signals for robust prioritization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content-level red flags (text, data, and images)
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts generated or handled by paper mills often show content issues like awkward phrasing, vague/missing hypotheses, image integrity problems, reagent errors, and lack of raw data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These issues may pass automated checks but often require skeptical human review. Look for template-like wording, repeated figure patterns, implausible experimental details, and absence of underlying data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangulate evidence before public accusation
rubrics_metrics.description: Before publicly asserting a paper is fraudulent, assemble multiple lines of evidence and, where possible, allow authors and publishers to comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The investigators withheld a public database until authors had opportunity to respond; share findings with journals/publishers and seek their internal review before public release. Preserve documentation and reconstruction evidence (Wayback snapshots, scraped contracts) to support claims.
